pogson.l1: Proxima Centauri: {f:proxima}; its light takes {f:proximaLy} years.
pogson.l2: Since Hipparchus, stars were sorted into six magnitudes — by eye.
pogson.l3: Pogson, {f:pogsonYear}: five magnitudes are exactly ×100; one step ≈ ×{f:pogsonStep}.
pogson.l4: Every star here is drawn by this formula — as seen from where the camera is now.
pogson.note: Flux follows Pogson; the screen shows its logarithm, the way the eye perceives it.

napier.l1: 1614. John Napier publishes the “Description of the Wonderful Table of Logarithms”.
napier.l2: His idea: multiplication turns into addition.
napier.l3: Henry Briggs makes logarithms decimal: log 10 = 1. That is our scale.
napier.l4: Kepler computes the “Rudolphine Tables” (1627) with them. Laplace is credited with saying logarithms “doubled the life of astronomers”.
napier.tableNote: Values computed from Napier’s definition L = 10⁷·ln(10⁷/sin); not a copy of the printed page.
orbit.l1: {f:karman} is the conventional edge of space; the ISS flies at ≈ {f:issAlt}.
orbit.l2: Staying in orbit takes ≈ {f:vOrbit}; with ascent losses, ≈ {f:dvLeo}.
orbit.l3: Speed grows as the logarithm of mass: to double Δv, you must square the mass ratio.
orbit.l4: That is why a rocket is almost all fuel: with vₑ ≈ {f:ve} it is ≈ {f:fuelPct} % of the launch mass (an ideal single stage).
moon.l1: The Moon is {f:moonDist} away — light takes {f:moonLight} s.
moon.l2: Sizes here are true: at this scale the Earth and the Moon are almost dots.
moon.l3: Full Moon −12.7ᵐ, Sun −26.7ᵐ. How much brighter is the Sun? We will work it out eight orders of magnitude from here.
au.l1: 1 au ≈ {f:au}: sunlight takes {f:sunLightMin} min {f:sunLightSec} s to reach us.
au.l2: The planets are where they are today — from JPL orbital elements.
au.l3: Distances are true; planet sizes are enlarged, or you would not see them.
kepler.l1: 1619. Kepler: the square of the orbital period equals the cube of the orbit size (T in years, a in au).
kepler.l2: Take logarithms — and the power becomes a factor.
kepler.l3: On logarithmic axes all the planets fall on one straight line of slope 3/2.
hr.l1: Let us rearrange the stars: colour across, luminosity up.
hr.l2: Each star’s absolute magnitude M comes from the distance modulus.
hr.l3: Luminosities span 10⁻⁴ to 10⁶ suns. Only a logarithmic axis can hold them.
hr.note: HYG stars within 300 pc. Both axes are logarithmic: M = −2.5·log₁₀ L + const.
weber.l1: Why did a scale made “by eye” turn out logarithmic?
weber.l2: Sensation grows roughly as the logarithm of the stimulus.
weber.l3: Hearing works the same way: an octave is ×2 in frequency, and each one sounds the same “step” higher.
weber.note: For brightness Stevens’ power law is more accurate; Fechner’s logarithm is a good first approximation.
mw.l1: The Milky Way’s disc is about {f:mwDisk} across, with hundreds of billions of stars.
mw.l2: Its arms are close to a logarithmic spiral.
mw.l3: Its secret is a constant pitch angle. Ours is ≈ {f:pitch}°, so b = tan {f:pitch}° ≈ {f:tanPitch}.
mw.l4: This galaxy is built from the same formula: the model is schematic, the angle is real.
m31.l1: 1920: was it a cloud inside our Galaxy or another “island universe”?
m31.l2: Leavitt, 1912: a Cepheid’s luminosity depends linearly on the logarithm of its period.
m31.l3: 1923: Hubble finds a Cepheid in Andromeda with a period of ≈ {f:v1Period} days and marks the plate “VAR!”.
m31.l4: The distance modulus gives the answer: then ≈ 900,000 light-years, today ≈ 2.5 million — another galaxy.
m31.label: Andromeda Galaxy · M31
uni.l1: ≈ {f:universeDiam} — the diameter of the observable Universe.
uni.l2: Beyond lies light that has not yet had time to reach us.
uni.l3: If the scroll were linear (1 pixel = 1 m, 1000 px/s), crossing this diameter would take ≈ {f:scrollYears} years — {f:scrollVsAge} times the age of the Universe.
map.kicker: The whole journey at a glance
map.l1: Each ring is ×10. Twenty-seven rings — from you to the edge.
map.l2: On this map, multiplying a distance means stepping out by a ring.
map.note: The logarithmic map idea: J. R. Gott, M. Jurić et al., “A Map of the Universe” (2005).

keplerTool.l1: Kepler knew six planets. The law also holds for Ceres, Pluto and Halley’s Comet.
kepler.hint: Drag your own planet: its period is T = a^(3/2).
kepler.boxcox: The axes morph via (x^λ − 1)/λ: as λ → 0 it becomes ln x.
rule.l1: Now the ruler is in your hands.
rule.l2: Put the “1” of slide C over a on scale D — under b on C read a·b.
rule.l3: Shifting the scales adds logarithms: log a + log b = log(a·b).
rule.l4: Slide rules flew on Apollo: a pocket Pickett N600-ES went to the Moon on Apollo 11.
rule.title: Slide rule
rule.hint: Drag slide C and the cursor with the mouse or the arrow keys.
rule.mars1: Step 1: cursor on 1.524 on scale A — read √1.524 ≈ 1.234 on D.
rule.mars2: Step 2: slide index over 1.234, cursor on 1.524 on C — read 1.88 on D.
rule.mars3: T = a·√a = a^(3/2) ≈ 1.88 years — Mars’s real period.
weber.linNote: 220 · 440 · 660 · 880 Hz — the steps sound smaller and smaller

egg.spira1: Jacob Bernoulli asked for a logarithmic spiral on his tombstone with the words “Eadem mutata resurgo” — “Changed, I rise again the same”.
egg.spira2: Scaling cannot change it: stretching by e^(2πb) is the same as turning it by 360°.
egg.spira3: The stonemason got it wrong and carved an Archimedean spiral r = aθ. It is still in Basel Minster.
